Maria Altshuller1,6, Guojun Shi 2,6, Victoria A. MacKrell1, Jasmine Tzeng1, Richa Nigam1, Jade K. Konsler1, Ting-Yu Wang3,4, Yixing Wang2, Emma J. Grogan5, Obehi E. Ozua5, Judith L. Campbell1,3, James M. Dewar 5, Tsui-Fen Chou 3,4, Binghui Shen 2 & Daniel R. Semlow 1

During replication-coupled DNA interstrand cross-link (ICL) repair, fork reversal is thought to enable the Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway to resolve the ICL through nucleolytic incisions. The resulting regressed arm of the reversed fork undergoes extensive nucleolytic resection that may facilitate completion of replication. Despite the importance of these remodeling events, their regulation remains poorly understood. Here, we use cell-free Xenopus egg extracts and human cells to investigate reversed fork processing during ICL repair by the FA pathway. We ﬁnd that the ataxia telangiectasia-mutated (ATM) kinase is activated concomitantly with fork reversal and promotes resection of reversed fork intermediates. ATM enhances chromatin recruitment of DNA2, which acts alongside EXO1 to resect reversed forks formed during ICL repair. Moreover, inhibition of protein phosphatase 2 A (PP2A) leads to ATM hyperactivation, accelerated reversed fork processing, and accumulation of aberrant end-joining products, implying that PP2A restrains ATM signaling to limit reversed fork resection. Taken together, this work identiﬁes reversed forks as substrates for ATM activation and reveals a phospho-regulatory circuit that controls reversed fork processing.

DNA interstrand cross-links (ICLs) covalently link the two strands of DNA and thereby block strand separation. These lesions are produced by endogenous cellular metabolites (e.g., formaldehyde, crotonaldehyde, abasic sites), microbiome-derived secondary metabolites (e.g., colibactin), and chemotherapeutics (e.g., cisplatin, nitrogen mustard derivatives, psoralens)1,2. Mutations in genes associated with ICL repair cause human diseases, including chronic kidney disease, karyomegalic interstitial nephritis and the bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition syndrome Fanconi anemia1,3. ICLs represent formidable impediments to DNA replication and can lead to deletions,

chromosomal rearrangements, and chromosome missegregation. Consequently, even a single unrepaired ICL can be lethal to a eukaryotic cell4. Among the multiple mechanisms that cells have evolved to resolve ICLs, the Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway is thought to be the most important for ICL resistance in proliferating cells1. The FA pathway is coupled to DNA replication and can be triggered by the convergence and stalling of replisomes on either side of an ICL (Fig. 1a)5. A second nuclease, such as SNM1A, mediates 5’ to 3’ expansion of the XPF-induced nick past the ICL to release (“unhook”) the cross-link and generate a DNA double-strand break (DSB). Subsequent steps in ICL repair are less well-deﬁned. However, resolution of the reversed fork is likely required to deliver the 3’ end of the nascent leading strand up to the ICL, allowing translesion synthesis (TLS) past the unhooked ICL adduct (“ICL remnant”) and completion of replication on one sister chromatid11,12. The two-ended DSB produced upon unhooking and reversed fork resolution is then repaired by homologous recombination using the fully-replicated sister chromatid as a template13. While current evidence indicates that replication fork reversal and subsequent reversed fork resolution are integral steps in ICL repair by the FA pathway, little is known about the enzymes that execute these fork dynamics or how they are regulated. The enzyme that mediates fork reversal in the FA pathway has not been identiﬁed, though the FANCM translocase is a likely candidate14. The factors responsible for reversed fork resolution during ICL repair are also unknown, but this process may depend on one or more RecQ family translocases. The RecQ family members WRN and BLM can resolve model reversed fork substrates in vitro15,16, and RECQ1 promotes reversed fork resolution in response to camptothecin-induced replication stress17. Reversed fork resolution during ICL repair may also depend on nuclease activities. For instance, the DNA2 nuclease-helicase and WRN helicase are known to act cooperatively to perform 5’ to 3’ resection of reversed fork regressed arms and promote replication restart following replication stress18. Currently, the mechanisms that regulate fork reversal and resolution are not fully understood. Emerging evidence suggests that the ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) kinase regulates the replication stress response19–21. ATM is canonically activated at DSB ends through interactions with the MRE11- RAD50-NBS1 (MRN) nuclease complex and promotes resection and RAD51 ﬁlament formation at DSBs22–24. ATM thereby stimulates homology-directed repair of two-ended DSBs as well as one-ended DSBs generated upon replication fork collapse25–27. Conversely, ATM has also been shown to phosphorylate 53BP1, which promotes 53BP1’s interaction with RIF1 and thereby constrains resection of DSB ends28,29. ATM may therefore tune the extent of DSB end processing to ensure efﬁcient repair. Intriguingly, genetic interactions between ATM and fork reversal and processing factors provide indirect evidence that the regressed arms of reversed fork structures can also activate ATM30–32. Importantly, these studies indicated that ATM constrains nuclease activity to prevent reversed fork degradation and enable recovery from replication stress30. It is unclear whether ATM also promotes resection of reversed forks, as it does at canonical DSB ends. In addition, how the ATM itself is regulated in response to replication stress has not been determined. Here, we used genome-wide CRISPR dropout screens and cell-free Xenopus egg extracts that faithfully model replication-coupled ICL repair to uncover a role for ATM checkpoint kinase signaling in regulating reversed fork processing during ICL repair. We show that protein phosphatase inhibition disrupts ICL repair by the FA pathway by inducing aberrant processing of reversed fork intermediates that is suppressed by ATM inhibition. We further show that ATM is normally activated upon replication fork reversal and promotes resection of nascent DNA strands, which depends on MRN, DNA2, WRN, and EXO1. Our results support a model in which the regressed arm of a reversed fork functions as a one-ended DSB that activates ATM to promote resection of the regressed arm. Our ﬁndings identify a role for ATM in regulating replication fork dynamics during ICL repair by the FA pathway.

Results Chemogenomic screens indicate a role for PP2A during ICL repair by the FA pathway To identify novel factors that participate in ICL repair by either the FA pathway or alternative repair pathways, we performed genome-wide chemogenomic CRISPR dropout screens with human hTERT-immortalized, p53-deﬁcient RPE-1 cells (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 1a, b)33. Cells were serially challenged with either UVA (control arm) or psoralen and UVA (PUVA; treatment arm), which together induce the formation of psoralen-ICLs that are known to be repaired by both the FA pathway and an alternative pathway mediated by the NEIL3 glycosylase7,8,34. Screens were performed using both FA pathwayproﬁcient cells (FANCD2+/+) and isogenic FA pathway-deﬁcient cells (FANCD2-/-), enabling us to distinguish genes that function epistatically with the FA pathway (only conferring PUVA resistance in the FA pathway-proﬁcient cells) from those that might function in alternative ICL repair pathways (conferring PUVA resistance in both FANCD2- proﬁcient and -deﬁcient cells). Validating our approach, we recovered 16 known FANC genes as ICL resistance genes in FANCD2-proﬁcient cells (Fig. 1c). Importantly, except for FANCJ, none of these genes were recovered as hits in the dropout screen performed with FANCD2- deﬁcient cells, consistent with roles for these genes in the same ICL repair pathway as FANCD2. Conversely, NEIL3 and FAN1, both of which can act independently of the FA pathway to promote ICL repair3,7,34,35, were recovered as ICL resistance genes in both FANCD2-proﬁcient and -deﬁcient cells. In addition to known FANC genes, PTPA emerged as an ICL resistance gene speciﬁcally in FANCD2-proﬁcient cells. Since PTPA encodes a factor that promotes PP2A phosphatase holoenzyme formation through activation of the PP2A catalytic subunit36, this result suggests that PP2A promotes ICL repair by the FA pathway. Note that genes encoding PP2A subunits (e.g., PP2A-A and PP2A-C) are essential and would therefore be unlikely to emerge as hits in CRISPR dropout screens37. Consistently, another set of genome-wide screens also implicated PTPA in resistance to cisplatin, which induces ICLs that require the FA pathway for replication-coupled repair33. In addition, PP2A-dependent FANCD2 dephosphorylation has been shown to be critical for FANCD2 ubiquitylation and activation of the FA pathway38. We therefore speciﬁcally tested whether PTPA contributes to ICL resistance. PTPA sgRNA knockout cell pools exhibited increased sensitivity to cisplatin (Fig. 1d, e), conﬁrming a role for PTPA in cellular tolerance to cisplatin-induced DNA damage. Overall, these results imply that PTPA activates PP2A to promote ICL repair by the FA pathway.

PP2A inhibition induces aberrant reversed replication fork processing To determine how PP2A phosphatase activity might regulate replication-coupled ICL repair, we replicated undamaged and ICLcontaining plasmids in Xenopus egg extracts supplemented with the pan-phosphoprotein phosphatase (PPPase) inhibitor okadaic acid. Following replication in the presence of [α-32P]dCTP (which is incorporated into the nascent DNA strands), replication intermediates and products were deproteinized and resolved by native agarose gel electrophoresis (Fig. 2a). In contrast, okadaic acid disrupted replication-coupled repair of a plasmid containing a cisplatin-ICL (pICLPt) that is repaired by the FA pathway40. We next considered the possibility that PP2A inhibition disrupts reversed fork processing by preventing FANCD2 dephosphorylation, which is required for efﬁcient FANCD2 monoubiquitylation and activation of the FA pathway38. Failure to dephosphorylate FANCD2 could promote reversed fork degradation by impairing productive ICL unhooking or by compromising FANCD2-dependent reversed fork protection42. However, addition of okadaic acid did not inhibit the accumulation of monoubiquitylated FANCD2 during pICLPt replication in egg extract (Supplementary Fig. 2f), indicating that PP2A inhibition does not suppress FANCD2 ubiquitylation in this system. Moreover, we and others have shown that FANCD2 depletion generally stabilizes reversed fork intermediates during replication-coupled repair of diverse ICLs7,43,44. The effects of okadaic acid are therefore distinct from those caused by loss of FANCD2 monoubiquitylation. Together, these observations suggest that okadaic acid corrupts reversed fork processing through an alternative mechanism in egg extract. To better understand how okadaic acid disrupts ICL repair by the FA pathway, we monitored the stability and maturation of the nascent DNA strands during ICL repair. pICLPt was replicated in egg extract supplemented with [α-32P]dCTP and okadaic acid, as indicated, and recovered replication intermediates were digested with restriction enzymes that allow the nascent DNA leading strands to be resolved on a denaturing sequencing gel (Fig. 2c). In the absence of okadaic acid, nascent leading strands initially stalled 20 to 40 nucleotides (nt) upstream of the ICL (−20 to −40 stall) due to the footprint of CMG. Upon CMG unloading, the nascent strands were extended up to 1 nt

upstream of the ICL (−1 stall). ICL unhooking and TLS past the resulting ICL remnant converted the nascent leading strands into fulllength extension products. In the presence of okadaic acid, nascent leading strands ﬁrst stalled at −20 to −40 before being extended to the −1 position. However, okadaic acid treatment induced a rapid disappearance of nascent leading strand −1 stall products. This loss of leading strand stall products was accompanied by both a decrease in formation of the expected nascent strand extension product and an increase in the formation of nascent strand extension products that were predominantly shorter than the expected product, suggesting that excessive okadaic acid-induced processing of replication intermediates leads to fork collapse and/or formation of deletion-prone end-joining products. Okadaic acid treatment also accelerated the disappearance of nascent lagging strand stall products (Fig. 2d; compare lanes 1 and 2 with lanes 5 and 6). Sequencing of pICLPt replication products recovered from untreated or okadaic acid-treated extracts conﬁrmed that okadaic acid treatment caused a reduction in the fraction of sequencing reads corresponding to error-free repair products and a substantial increase in the fraction of reads with deletions spanning the ICL (Fig. 2e). Taken together, our results support a model in which PP2A stabilizes reversed fork repair intermediates by restraining nucleolytic processing or error-prone end-joining of these intermediates. PP2A has been reported to physically interact with BRCA2 and promote RAD51 loading at DSBs45. Since RAD51 ﬁlaments antagonize reversed fork degradation by DNA2 and MRN46,47, we wondered if a deﬁcit in fork protection caused by inefﬁcient RAD51 loading leads to excessive reversed fork intermediate processing in okadaic acidtreated extracts. replication reactions (Fig. 2f). We next tested whether disruption of RAD51 loading is sufﬁcient to destabilize reversed fork intermediates formed during replication-coupled ICL repair. As previously observed13, addition of BRC4 peptide that blocks the interaction between RAD51 and BRCA2 prevented RAD51 loading during replication of pICLPt (Supplementary Fig. 2g). Importantly, the BRC4 peptide did not inhibit fork reversal, indicating that RAD51 is dispensable for fork reversal following CMG unloading at an ICL in egg extract. This ﬁnding is consistent with previous work, which demonstrated that RAD51 is not required for fork reversal when CMG has been displaced from chromatin48. Addition of BRC4 peptide did not destabilize reversed fork intermediates (Fig. 2g), indicating that loss of RAD51- dependent forkprotection is not sufﬁcient to induce aberrant reversed fork processing during ICL repair in egg extract. MRN has also been implicated in the processing of reversed forks. We therefore tested whether reversed fork processing during ICL repair requires MRN. MRE11 depletion stabilized reversed fork intermediates during pICLPt replication in extract (Fig. 6a, b), suggesting that MRN either mediates ATM activation at reversed forks or directly participates in resection of regressed arms. Similar stabilization of reversed fork intermediates was observed upon NBS1 depletion (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). Importantly, MRE11 depletion also suppressed ATM S1981 phosphorylation (Fig. 6c), indicating that MRN contributes to reversed fork processing during ICL repair at least in part by promoting ATM activation. To identify additional potential effectors of ATM-dependent reversed fork processing, we proﬁled the phosphoproteome during pICLPt replication in untreated and okadaic acid-treated extracts. Okadaic acid treatment resulted in a signiﬁcant, at least 2-fold increase in abundance for ~8.7% of phosphopeptides detected (Supplementary Fig. 6c–e). Several phosphopeptides that were signiﬁcantly enriched in okadaic acid-treated extract corresponded to the nucleases DNA2 and EXO1, as well as to the DNA2-associated helicases BLM and WRN. Since DNA2, WRN, and EXO1 have been previously implicated in reversed fork resection18,58, we tested whether they mediate processing during

ICL repair. Addition of the DNA2 inhibitor C559, the EXO1 inhibitor C20060, or the WRN inhibitor HRO76161 to extracts resulted in a strong accumulation of reversed fork intermediates and a decrease in the amount of fully replicated supercoiled products (Fig. 6d), mirroring the effects of ATM inhibition and suggesting that DNA2, WRN, and EXO1 process the reversed fork intermediates. Similar stabilization of reversed fork intermediates generated during ICL repair was also observed with the EXO1 inhibitor F68460 (Supplementary Fig. 6f). Combined inhibition of these factors produced a stronger stabilization of reversed fork intermediates than inhibition of any individual factor, suggesting that DNA2, WRN, and EXO1 may act redundantly in resecting reversed fork intermediates (Supplementary Fig. 6g). Inhibition of DNA2, WRN, or EXO1 also stabilized reversed fork intermediates and delayed the accumulation of putative fork collapse products in okadaic acid-treated extract (Fig. 6d), implying that these factors contribute to aberrant reversed fork processing in the absence of PP2A activity. We next examined the effects of DNA2, WRN, and EXO1 inhibition on nascent strand maturation. Like ATM inhibition, inhibition of DNA2, WRN, or EXO1 caused a strong persistence of −1 and 0 leading strand stall products and a corresponding reduction in the amount of fulllength extension products (Fig. 6e), suggesting that DNA2, WRN, and EXO1 might be required for reversed fork resolution and subsequent bypass of the unhooked ICL remnant. Inhibition of DNA2, WRN, or EXO1 also caused a strong persistence of nascent lagging strands, indicating that these nucleases promote 5’ to 3’ resection of reversed fork intermediates (Fig. 6f). Interestingly, EXO1 inhibition resulted in a more pronounced stabilization of the longest lagging strands with 5’ ends nearest to the end of the regressed arm of a reversed fork structure. By contrast, inhibition of DNA2 or WRN resulted in more pronounced stabilization of shorter lagging strands corresponding to recessed 5’ ends on the regressed arm of a reversed fork. These data suggest that EXO1 may initiate 5’ to 3’ resection at a reversed fork, after which DNA2 acts with WRN to further resect 5’ recessed ends. Discussion Although current data imply that replication fork reversal and reversed fork resolution are integral steps in ICL repair by the FA pathway, little is known about which factors mediate these fork dynamics or how they are regulated. Here, we used chemogenomic screens and Xenopus egg extracts to uncover a phosphoregulatory circuit involving ATM that contributes to reversed fork processing during ICL repair. A CRISPR dropout screen implicated the PP2A activator PTPA in ICL repair by the FA pathway. We then determined that inhibition of PP2A activity results in hyperactivation of ATM and is associated with destabilization of reversed fork intermediates, fork collapse, and formation of deletion-prone end-joining products. Our data indicate that ATM is activated concurrently with fork reversal and that this activation promotes resection of regressed arms (Fig. 7a). These observations

indicate that ATM directs resection of reversed forks in a manner that is counteracted by phosphatase activity. We further implicate the resection enzymes MRN, DNA2-WRN, and EXO1 in mediating this resection, implying that these factors are directly or indirectly activated by ATM at a reversed fork. Thus, our results indicate that the regressed arm of a reversed fork formed during ICL repair triggers ATM signaling, thereby enhancing processing of this structure. Given that replication fork reversal is a frequent response to diverse replication stresses62, ATM may be a key regulator of replication fork dynamics during replication stress. A recent report demonstrated that chromatin-bound cGAS promotes replication fork reversal while ATM counteracts this reversal63. In this case, ATM appears to target conserved phosphorylation sites on MRE11 (S676 and S678) to stimulate MRN-dependent reversed fork processing and enable replication restart. In addition to phosphorylating the MRN complex, ATM is known to phosphorylate EXO1 and to physically interact with DNA264,65. ATM also phosphorylates the WRN and BLM helicases, both of which stimulate DNA2-dependent resection and have been implicated in the processing of reversed forks18,66–71. Our data therefore suggest that ATM may directly activate DNA2, WRN, and/or EXO1 to stimulate resection at reversed forks, either by stimulating the activity of these enzymes or by promoting their recruitment to reversed forks. ATM may also contribute to reversed fork resection by more indirect mechanisms, such as by enabling displacement of the anti-resection factor 53BP1 from chromatin or by enhancing ATR activation through phosphorylation of TOPBP172–74. Conversely, ATM has also been reported to stabilize reversed forks – for instance, MRE11 phosphorylation by ATM facilitates MRN release from chromatin and prevents the degradation of reversed forks30–32. Combined with this previous report, our results indicate that ATM may regulate multiple stages of resection to tune reversed fork processing, promoting sufﬁcient resection for replication restart while avoiding excessive resection and consequent fork collapse (Fig. 7a). PP2A also appears to regulate multiple facets of ICL repair. PP2A enables efﬁcient ubiquitylation and chromatin recruitment of the FANCI-FANCD2 complex at ICLs38. PP2A also interacts with BRCA2 to promote RAD51 ﬁlament formation during homologous recombination45, suggesting that it may contribute to fork protection during ICL repair or facilitate repair of the DSB intermediate generated by FANCI-FANCD2-dependent ICL unhooking. Our data now reveal a distinct function for PP2A that contributes to efﬁcient ICL repair. By counteracting ATM activation, PP2A prevents excessive processing of reversed fork intermediates. Notably, while reversed forks underwent rapid processing upon PP2A inhibition, reversed forks were not destabilized by inactivation of either FANCD2 or RAD51 (Figs. 2b, g and 5c), both of which contribute to fork protection during ICL repair42,75. Thus, in egg extracts, PP2A may preserve fork integrity primarily by suppressing ATM-stimulated resection rather than by enhancing fork protection pathways. These ﬁndings further indicate that multiple phosphatases cooperate to limit resection at reversed forks. The RIF1- PP1 complex, for example, dephosphorylates WRN and suppresses DNA2-WRN-dependent fork degradation76,77. We propose that PP2A and RIF1-PP1 may act in concert to restrain pathological fork resection during ICL repair, possibly alongside additional phosphatase activities. A key outstanding question concerns how ATM-stimulated reversed fork processing might promote reversed fork resolution and completion of ICL repair. We can envision multiple possibilities. 5’ to 3’ resection of the nascent lagging strand could allow RAD51 to load onto the resulting 3’ overhang and mediate invasion of the parental DNA duplex, generating a joint molecule structure with the nascent leading strand poised for extension past the unhooked ICL remnant (Fig. 7b, left). While this idea may be consistent with available data, evidence for the formation of strand invasion intermediates predicted by this model is currently lacking9. 5’ to 3’ resection could also act in concert with a 3’ to 5’ exonuclease or 3’ ﬂap endonuclease that degrades the 3’ overhang, eventually regenerating a replication fork with a free 3’ end that can be extended through the parental DNA duplex and past the ICL remnant (Fig. 7b, middle). Consistent with this model, our TEM data indicate that both strands of the reversed fork regressed arms are resected during ICL repair (Fig. 4). It is worth noting that DNA2, which our data implicate in reversed forkprocessing during ICL repair, has robust 3’ to 5’ nuclease activity that can, in some contexts, mediate nascent leading strand degradation at a reversed fork78,79. Resection of the regressed arm might also cooperate with branch migration to facilitate fork resolution by a DNA translocase, such as a member of the RecQ family (Fig. 7b, right). If targeted to both

strands of the regressed arm, resection would reduce the distance of branch migration required before a replication fork is restored. ATMdependent reversed fork processing could also indirectly favor fork resolution by antagonizing toxic non-homologous end-joining of reversed fork regressed arms80,81. Our ﬁnding that ATM regulates reversed fork processing during ICL repair predicts that ATM deﬁciency should confer sensitivity to ICL-inducing agents. Current data indicate that, although ATM inhibition enhances sensitivity to cisplatin and other ICL-inducing agents in some cell lines, this effect is not universal82–86. ATM may therefore be strictly required for ICL resistance only in certain contexts or in combination with genetic deﬁciencies, such as loss of PTEN or BRCA1/2. Notably, ATM inhibition strongly synergizes with deﬁciencies in the FA pathway, a ﬁnding that has been attributed to an inability to activate homologous recombination and suppress toxic non-homologous endjoining87. However, these data do not preclude a function for ATM at earlier stages of ICL repair in mammalian cells. Our results also suggest a mechanistic basis for understanding previously reported genetic interactions between DNA2 and the FA pathway. DNA2 depletion induces hypersensitivity to cisplatin, implying that DNA2-mediated resection is required during ICL repair88. Counterintuitively, DNA2 depletion suppresses ICL sensitivity in FANCD2-deﬁcient cells, indicating that DNA2-dependent resection of ICL repair intermediates can corrupt ICL repair when the FANCD2 function is compromised89. We propose that DNA2 deﬁciency can suppress defects in the FA pathway by extending the window during which unhooking can occur before nonproductive reversed fork processing renders the ICL refractory to repair. This model suggests that manipulating the balance between fork reversal and reversed fork processing could have therapeutic beneﬁts in FA patients. Inhibitors of reversed fork processing factors, including DNA2 and ATM, could stabilize reversed fork intermediates to facilitate ICL unhooking by a compromised FA pathway. It may also be possible to dampen reversed fork processing and rescue ICL repair using small molecule activators of PP2A90.

Error-free repair assay Error-free repair was quantiﬁed essentially as described previously98. Brieﬂy, pICLPt was replicated as described above alongside an undamaged plasmid (pQuant), which is used as an internal loading control in downstream analysis. Deproteinized replication intermediates were puriﬁed as described above, and 2 µL of recovered DNA was digested with either 2 U HincII or 2 U each of HincII and SapI (NEB #R0569) in 1X NEBuffer rCutSmart at 37 °C for 3 h. Digestion products were resolved on a native 0.8% agarose gel and visualized by phosphorimaging. Since the SapI recognition site overlaps with the cisplatin-ICL, error-free repair of the cross-link can be monitored by the restoration of SapI cleavage. The intensity of the HincII/SapI double digestion products was quantiﬁed in Image Lab (v6.1.0) and normalized to the corresponding pQuant intensity in each lane. To exclude confounding signal from incision products that form during FA pathway-dependent repair, the intensities of HincII single digestion products were subtracted from the intensities of HincII/SapI double digestion products. The percentage of the replicated plasmid that underwent error-free repair was determined by calculating the proportion of normalized digestion products to total replicated pICLPt (quantiﬁed by multiplying the pQuant band intensity by its dilution factor compared to pICLPt)98.

Proteomic data analysis RAW ﬁles were processed using the CHIMERYS103 intelligent search algorithm with Inferys 4.7.0 fragmentation prediction (version 4.0, MSAID GmbH) in Proteome Discoverer (PD) (v3.2; Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc) against the 10.1 version of the Xenopus laevis genome downloaded from Xenbase (https://wuehr.scholar.princeton.edu/sites/g/ ﬁles/toruqf2761/ﬁles/xenla_10_1_xenbase.fasta.txt). Peptides between 7 and 30 amino acids were considered, and the false discovery rate (FDR) for peptide spectra matches (PSMs) identiﬁcations was set to 1%. Quantiﬁcation type was set to MS2 Apex. Data were deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identiﬁer PXD071242104. Differential abundance analysis between control and okadaic acid-treated samples was performed using linear mixed-effects models, which estimated Log2 fold changes (Log2FCs) and p-values for each phosphosite. Resulting p-values were adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure107. Phosphosites with FDR-adjusted p-values < 0.05 and absolute Log₂FC > 0.5 were considered signiﬁcantly regulated. # Synthesis of 6-epi-Hypersampsone R by a Desymmetrization Strategy

**Authors:** Marva Tariq; Trevor W Butcher; Scott C Virgil; Brian M Stoltz

**Affiliations:** 1 The Warren and Katharine Schlinger Laboratory for Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, United States

## Abstract

We report an approach to hypersampsone R that results in a 10-step synthesis of 6-epi-hypersampsone R, a polycyclic polyprenylated acylphloroglucinol (PPAP) possessing a rare bicyclo[3.3.1]­nonane-2–8-dione core. This strategy includes a high-yielding and scalable synthesis of an achiral [3.3.1] bicyclic bis-enone that is further elaborated via bridgehead functionalization and desymmetrization. The synthesis is completed through a one-pot conjugate addition/acylation strategy to construct the final two carbon–carbon bonds. Overall, the general strategy of (i) core synthesis, (ii) desymmetrization, and (iii) functionalization outlined herein may provide a general platform for the synthesis of structurally related PPAPs.

## Abstract

## Abstract

Polycyclic polyprenylated acylphloroglucinols (PPAPs) are a class of diverse bioactive natural products isolated from the plants of the Guttiferae family. To date, nearly 1400 PPAPs have been isolated, and numerous PPAPs are known to exhibit anticancer, antidepressant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antioxidant, and antiviral activities. In addition to their significant bioactivities, PPAPs possess complex molecular structures, making them attractive targets for chemical synthesis.

Given the large number of isolated PPAPs, these molecules can be further distinguished by their diverse cores. A majority of PPAPs exhibit a bicyclo[3.3.1]­nonane core bearing oxidation at C2, C4, and C9 (Figure , top left) and are now commonly termed bicylic polyprenylated acylphloroglucinols (BPAPs). The most widely known BPAP, hyperforin (1), is the active constituent in St. John’s Wort, an herbal antidepressant that is clinically used across Europe. PPAPs also include compounds featuring adamantane or homoadamantane cores, and several noteworthy syntheses have been directed toward these scaffolds.

*1: Different PPAP scaffolds (top) and representative PPAPs (bottom).*

Among BPAPs, nearly all possess oxidation at the C2, C4, and C9 sites of the bicyclic core. However, in 2014, chemists in Taiwan isolated hypersampsone R (2), a unique BPAP exhibiting oxidation at positions C2 and C8 of the bicycle. Additionally, hypersampsone R has four stereocenters, including one quaternary stereocenter. Although the bioactivity of this natural product is unknown, the breadth of bioactivities exhibited by PPAPs is a result of subtle variations in the identity, position, and configuration of the substituents decorating the polycyclic core. Given this rare oxidation pattern, paired with other structural complexities, we sought to synthesize hypersampsone R. To the best of our knowledge, there have been no reports directed toward the synthesis of either hypersampsone R (2) or 6-epi-hypersampsone R (3).

We planned to achieve the synthesis of hypersampsone R (2) by focusing on the construction of a key bicyclic intermediate that would allow for the late-stage installation of all four appendages. After retrosynthetically disconnecting the peripheral groups of hypersampsone R, the underlying symmetry present within the natural product becomes readily apparent (Scheme , top). We proposed that achiral bicycle 4 would serve as a key intermediate that would allow for late-stage functionalization of the core. We hypothesized that this symmetry-guided approach would greatly simplify the construction of the core. Additionally, we envisioned that deferring the installation of each appendage to the end of the synthesis could enable a general route to a variety of potential analogues from a single intermediate.

*1: Uncovering the Hidden Symmetry of Hypersampsone R (2) (top) and Retrosynthetic Analysis of Hypersampsone R (2) (bottom)*

Starting from hypersampsone R (2), retrosynthetically disconnecting the tautomeric benzoyl group at C7 and the prenyl group at C3 reveals enone 5 (Scheme , bottom). We then proposed that the isobutenyl group at C6 could be introduced via a transition-metal-catalyzed enantio-, diastereo-, and monoselective conjugate addition to desymmetrize dienone 6. With our key intermediate in mind, we envisioned that the prenyl group at C1 could be installed via bridgehead lithiation, followed by in situ prenylation. Redox manipulation of our key intermediate (4) delivers alcohol 7. We envisioned that bicyclic alcohol 7 could be produced via an intramolecular aldol reaction of aldehyde 8. To access compound 8, we planned to employ an alkylation and Stork–Danheiser sequence originating from vinylogous ester 9, which can be derived from commercially available dimedone (10).

We began our forward synthesis by converting dimedone into vinylogous ester 9, which proceeded in 84% yield on 100 g scale (Scheme ). After preliminary investigations of the ideal aldehyde precursor, we concluded that a terminal alkyne was the optimal functional handle and constructed alkyne 11 in 88% yield. Compound 11 was then subjected to Stork–Danheiser transposition followed by a Ru-catalyzed anti-Markovnikov alkyne hydration to produce aldehyde 8 in 95% yield on a multigram scale. , Aldehyde 8 underwent an acid-promoted intramolecular aldol reaction to produce bicycle 7 as a single diastereomer in 90% yield. Oxidation of alcohol 7 with Dess-Martin periodinane and desaturation of the resulting ketone-derived enolate with Mukaiyama’s reagent produced dienone 4 in 52% yield. In total, key intermediate 4 was produced in seven steps. The first step was performed on a large scale, and we prepared more than 100 g of vinylogous ester 9 and 84 g of propargyl substrate 11 via distillation. The remaining steps toward aldol product 7 were conducted on a smaller scale, and 8 g of bicycle 7 was obtained without the need for silica gel flash chromatography following neutralization with bicarbonate and extraction into EtOAc. Oxidation and desaturation of alcohol 7 were also achieved on a gram scale. Overall, the synthesis of key intermediate 4 is concise, high yielding, and reasonably scalable.

*2: Forward Synthesis of Key Intermediate 4 and Subsequent Bridgehead Prenylation*

With key intermediate 4 in hand, the bicycle was further manipulated in an effort to install the four substituents decorating the core of hypersampsone R. Although bridgehead prenylations of [3.3.1] bicycles are known from prior PPAP syntheses, we were concerned that the quaternary center of intermediate 4 might pose an issue for anion formation and/or subsequent prenylation. Nonetheless, inspired by previous reports of bridgehead functionalization on similar bicyclic systems, we decided to employ standard alkylation conditions to affect this transformation. To our delight, treatment of bis-enone 4 with LDA at −78 °C followed by prenyl bromide resulted in bridgehead prenylation affording bicycle 6 in 63% yield (Scheme ).

Desymmetrization of the prenylated bicycle (6) proved to be more challenging than we had anticipated. We proposed to install the isobutenyl group at C6 via asymmetric conjugate addition, establishing three stereocenters, including a quaternary stereocenter, in one step. Asymmetric conjugate additions that desymmetrize polycyclic ring systems are rare, and to the best of our knowledge, there are no asymmetric conjugate additions that can distinguish between two remote enones. However, given recent developments in rhodium-catalyzed asymmetric conjugate addition chemistry, we decided to pursue this approach. There is strong precedent that Rh-catalyzed conjugate addition reactions performed with chiral phosphoramidite olefin ligands typically proceed through chelated square planar Rh­(I) intermediates. We hypothesized that our dienone could chelate to rhodium, which would enforce addition from the endo face and enhance the rate of the first addition, potentially enabling us to achieve a diastereoselective and monoselective addition of the isobutenyl group. In 2007, Nakao and co-workers reported high yields and high enantioselectivities of conjugate addition products, which were achieved with rhodium and hydroxy organosilanes. Adopting their reaction conditions for our desymmetrization led to the formation of the desired product (i.e., 5) as a single diastereomer albeit in low yields (Table , entry 1). When the reaction was performed with a slight excess of ligand, we observed limited catalytic turnover with a 21% NMR yield of desired conjugate addition product 5. However, this reaction was not enantioselective, suggesting that there is background reactivity that does not involve the chiral ligand in product formation. Increasing the ligand loading to counter this background reactivity led to greater enantioselectivity, although with a diminished NMR yield of only 8% and no catalytic turnover (entry 2). In both experiments, we also detected the formation of monoenone 13, possibly resulting from insertion of a rhodium–hydride complex into the olefin. This competing pathway offers another explanation for the low yields observed in these reactions. Unfortunately, other phosphoramidite and monodentate ligands did not increase the yield or enantioselectivity of the desired product. Given these results, we decided to pursue alternative desymmetrization methods.

We first attempted alkylation via a Li enolate generated from a single 1,4-conjugate reduction of dienone 6 (Scheme , top). Importantly, compound 13 was then subjected to standard alkylation conditions to produce more of desired diprenylated bicycle 14 in 25% yield. The addition of HMPA to these reactions was necessary to prevent the formation of a rearranged bicycle (Supporting Information). Other minor products that were isolated in these reactions include an O-alkylated bicycle and a compound with both the O-alkylation and C-alkylation (see the Supporting Information). Since we observed the formation of bicycle 13 in our desymmetrization efforts, we hoped to access this compound enantioselectively. With diprenylated bicycle 14 in hand, we continued our forward synthesis toward the natural product. We envisioned access to the natural product via a tandem conjugate addition/acylation strategy. There are limited examples of such tandem processes involving alkenyl nucleophiles, with most reports employing alkyl and aryl nucleophiles. To our delight, by using stoichiometric copper iodide in combination with isobutenylmagnesium bromide, the transformation proceeded in 40% yield, forming two carbon–carbon bonds in one step (Scheme ). However, our experimental 1H NMR spectrum did not match the reported spectrum of natural hypersampsone R. Following detailed NMR analysis, we concluded that we had synthesized the C6 epimer of hypersampsone R (i.e., 3). Given the bridged nature of the bicyclo[3.3.1]­nonane core, nucleophiles are more likely to approach from the top face of the bicycle (as drawn) rather than from the more hindered endocyclic face, resulting in the formation of the C6 epimer.

*4: Tandem Conjugate Addition/Acylation Strategy to Construct the Final Two Carbon–Carbon Bonds in 6-epi-Hypersampsone R*

Overall, the first total synthesis of 6-epi-hypersampsone R (3) was accomplished in only 10 steps. We developed a robust seven-step synthesis of our key intermediate (4), which was further elaborated via desymmetrization and peripheral functionalization. Lastly, a one-pot conjugate addition/acylation strategy was employed to construct the final two carbon–carbon bonds in 6-epi-hypersampsone R (3).
